activities.caption: pair each concept with its job in the business
activities.name: atJobsMatch

config.prompt: Two numbers run the entire business — match each concept to its job:

pairs.right: the long-run average — sets the floor for the price
how far outcomes can wander — sizes the capital for bad years
a number between 0 and 1 measuring how likely an event is
shrinks the relative uncertainty — scale is the oldest risk-reduction technology

config.why: Every other idea in this lesson is elaboration on that pair: expectation prices, variance capitalises.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the 99 percent trap
activities.name: atBayesSpot

config.prompt: One line of this fraud-screening answer is wrong — click it:
lines: The model flags 99% of fraudulent claims and 5% of honest ones; 1% of all claims are fraudulent.
Out of 10,000 claims, 100 are fraudulent, and 99 of those get flagged.
5% of the 9,900 honest claims also get flagged — 495 false alarms.
Among the 594 flags, 99 are real fraud: 99 ÷ 594 ≈ 16.7 percent.
So a flagged claim is 99 percent likely to be fraudulent — the model catches 99% of fraud.
config.correction: A flagged claim is fraudulent only about 16.7% of the time — honest claims vastly outnumber fraudulent ones.
config.why: The 99% is the true-positive rate, not the probability the flag is right. Base rates rule: nearly five out of six flags are false alarms.

activities.anchor: what happens in the year the equation fails
activities.caption: file the pairs — may the probabilities multiply?
activities.name: atIndependenceBuckets

config.prompt: Independence is the licence to multiply. File each pairing:

items.label: car accidents by separate drivers in separate towns
fire losses across the flats of one building
two distant drivers' accidents on the same icy morning
2,000 similar policies each facing their own small fire chance

config.why: The test is the multiplication rule, never the vibe: learning one event must not change the probability of the other. One fire takes the whole floor; one icy morning takes both drivers.

activities.anchor: a fire that totals a factory must remain possible
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the distribution catalogue
activities.name: atDistCloze

config.text: The %%0%% counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials; the %%1%% counts rare events arriving at a steady rate; the %%2%% models waiting times and is memoryless; the %%3%% emerges when many small independent effects add up.
config.hint: One name per blank — counts, arrivals, waits, sums.

activities.anchor: the whole of Bayesian practice lives in the space between
activities.caption: true or false — evidence and updates
activities.name: atBayesJudge

statements.s: P(fraud given flag) equals P(flag given fraud).
statements.why: 17 percent vs 99 percent — the same evidence, two very different probabilities. Confusing them is the prosecutor's fallacy.

statements.s: The prosecutor's fallacy ignores how many other people also match.
statements.why: 'One-in-a-million match' says nothing about guilt while a million-odd people also match.

statements.s: A 99-percent-accurate test means a flagged claim is 99 percent likely to be fraudulent.
statements.why: Base rates rule the answer — here it is about 16.7 percent.

statements.s: Bayes' theorem converts 'probability of the evidence if the cause is true' into 'probability of the cause given the evidence'.
statements.why: That reversal is the whole trick — and it sounds like a formality until it earns its keep.

activities.anchor: pooling — not prediction — is insurance's core competence
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the pool's typical miss
activities.name: atSdEstimate

config.prompt: The village at scale: 2,000,000 dollars of expected claims, standard deviation about 195,000. Roughly what per cent of the expected total is that typical miss?
config.why: 195,000 ÷ 2,000,000 ≈ 10% — and quadrupling the book only doubles the standard deviation (√n), so the relative uncertainty halves.
config.context: That 1-over-√n shrinkage is the law of large numbers wearing a business suit.

activities.anchor: That is the whole profession in one sentence
activities.caption: bet first — the press release vs the rate filing
activities.name: atMeanPredict

config.q: A press release quotes the 'average claim', and the number is smaller than the expected loss in the rate filing. Why?
choices: Because the press release rounds down
Because heavy tails put the mean above the median — the typical claim is small, but rare enormous claims drag the mean up
Because the press release counts only claims that were actually paid
config.why: Most claims are fender-benders; the rare totals-a-factory claim really arrives and really must be paid. Price the mean, capitalise the tail.
